chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Safwan, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the slaughtering of the cow from the place of slaughter (al-manhar), so he said: 'For the cow, it is slaughter (dhabh), and whatever is slaughtered by cutting the throat (nahr) is not considered properly slaughtered (dhakī).'

key_terms.الْمَنْحَر: The place of slaughter; specifically refers to the method of cutting the neck/throat from above (typically for camels)
key_terms.ذَبْح: Slaughtering (specifically by cutting the throat, applicable to cows)
key_terms.نُحِرَ: Was slaughtered by nahr (cutting the neck/throat from above)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between dhabh and nahr in Shia jurisprudence for slaughtering animals?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Safwan ibn Yahya inquires of Imam al-Rida (AS) regarding the precise linguistic and legal distinctions between *dhabh* (cutting the throat, typically for cows) and *nahr* (cutting the neck from above, typically for camels). The Imam clarifies that while both are valid forms of slaughter, the specific terminology dictates the proper application; thus, using the term and method of *nahr* for a cow renders it not properly *dhakī* according to the specific juristic nuance discussed here. This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the interplay between linguistic precision and ritual validity in fiqh.
